# Here we define our best performing model for each of the 2 finetuned methods and get their corresponding matched sets, so we can then continue with the rest of the analysis to see whether treatment significantly explains outcomes for each of the methods.
```{r}
# Create matched set for final random forest (node size = 10, mtry = 3 , 300 trees) for further downstream analysis.
set.seed(42)
# Final, best balancing Random Forest:
rf.model  <- randomForest(treatment.swang ~ ., data = rf.data, ntree = 300, nodesize = 10, mtry = 3, importance = TRUE)
pscore.rf <- predict(rf.model, type = "prob")[, "1"]
psmatch.rf <- Match(Tr = rhc.selected$treatment.swang, M = 1, X = logit(pmin(pmax(pscore.rf, 0.005), 0.995)),
                    replace = FALSE, Weight = 2, caliper = 0.2)
matched_rf <- rhc.selected[unlist(psmatch.rf[c("index.treated", "index.control")]), ]


# Create matched set for final neural network (weight decay = 0.01, hidden size = 1) for further downstream analysis.
# Final, best balancing Neural Network:
m <- nnet(treatment.swang ~ ., data = nn.df, size = 1, decay = 0.01,
          trace = FALSE, maxit = 300, linout = FALSE) 
pscore.nn <- predict(m, newdata = nn.df, type = "raw")[, 1] 
psmatch.nn <- Match(Tr = rhc.selected$treatment.swang, M = 1, X = logit(pmin(pmax(pscore.nn, 0.005), 0.995)), replace = FALSE, Weight = 2, caliper = 0.2)
matched_nn <- rhc.selected[unlist(psmatch.nn[c("index.treated", "index.control")]), ]
```



#Next, we perform the downstream outcome statistical analysis for each of the three new methods. Note that even though we prefer the original GLM model for its simplicity and interpretibility, we perform the analysis for all three models for comparison anyways, since the balancing performance was very similar.

```{r}
print("===================================================")
set.seed(42) #For reproducibility of results
# First for the RF:
print("For the RF:")
y_trt.rf <- matched_rf$outcome.died[matched_rf$treatment.swang == 1]
y_con.rf <- matched_rf$outcome.died[matched_rf$treatment.swang == 0]

t.test(y_trt.rf - y_con.rf)                 # paired t-test, indicative only
table(y_trt.rf, y_con.rf)
mcnemar.test(table(y_trt.rf, y_con.rf))     # correct test for paired binary data

gmodel5 <- glm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = binomial, data = matched_rf)
summary(gmodel5)

# Doubly robust: adjust for the least well balanced variable
worst.rf <- rf.row$worst.var
gmodel6 <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome.died ~ treatment.swang +", worst.rf)), family = binomial, data = matched_rf)
summary(gmodel6)
sprintf("Odds ratio for treatment: %.4f", exp(coef(gmodel5)["treatment.swang"]))
sprintf("Odds ratio for treatment after adjusting for %s: %.4f", worst.rf, exp(coef(gmodel6)["treatment.swang"]))

effects <- data.frame(
  method      = c("Mahalanobis", "PS (glm)", "PS (random forest)"),
  pairs       = c(length(greedymatch$index.treated), length(psmatch$index.treated), length(psmatch.rf$index.treated)),
  mean.diff   = c(mean(y_trt - y_con), mean(y_trt.ps - y_con.ps), mean(y_trt.rf - y_con.rf)),
  OR          = exp(c(coef(gmodel1)["treatment.swang"], coef(gmodel3)["treatment.swang"], coef(gmodel5)["treatment.swang"])),
  OR.adjusted = exp(c(coef(gmodel2)["treatment.swang"], coef(gmodel4)["treatment.swang"], coef(gmodel6)["treatment.swang"])))
#print(effects, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)


# Next, for the neural network:
print("For the NN:")
y_trt.nn <- matched_nn$outcome.died[matched_nn$treatment.swang == 1]
y_con.nn <- matched_nn$outcome.died[matched_nn$treatment.swang == 0]

t.test(y_trt.nn - y_con.nn)
mcnemar.test(table(y_trt.nn, y_con.nn))

gmodel7 <- glm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = binomial, data = matched_nn)
summary(gmodel7)
worst.nn <- nn.row$worst.var
gmodel8 <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome.died ~ treatment.swang +", worst.nn)), family = binomial, data = matched_nn)
summary(gmodel8)

sprintf("OR (unadjusted): %.4f", exp(coef(gmodel7)["treatment.swang"]))
sprintf("OR (adjusted for %s): %.4f", worst.nn, exp(coef(gmodel8)["treatment.swang"]))

effects <- rbind(effects, data.frame(
  method       = "PS (neural net)",
  pairs        = length(psmatch.nn$index.treated),
  mean.diff    = mean(y_trt.nn - y_con.nn),
  OR           = exp(coef(gmodel7)["treatment.swang"]),
  OR.adjusted  = exp(coef(gmodel8)["treatment.swang"])))
#print(effects, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)

#Lastly, for the CPBS model:
print("For the CBPS:")
y_trt.cbps <- matched_cbps$outcome.died[matched_cbps$treatment.swang == 1]
y_con.cbps <- matched_cbps$outcome.died[matched_cbps$treatment.swang == 0]

t.test(y_trt.cbps - y_con.cbps)
mcnemar.test(table(y_trt.cbps, y_con.cbps))

gmodel9 <- glm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = binomial, data = matched_cbps)
summary(gmodel9)
worst.cbps <- rownames(smd_values_matched_cbps)[which.max(smd_values_matched_cbps)]
gmodel10 <- glm(as.formula(paste("outcome.died ~ treatment.swang +", worst.cbps)), family = binomial, data = matched_cbps)
summary(gmodel10)

sprintf("OR (unadjusted): %.4f", exp(coef(gmodel9)["treatment.swang"]))
sprintf("OR (adjusted for %s): %.4f", worst.cbps, exp(coef(gmodel10)["treatment.swang"]))

effects <- rbind(effects, data.frame(
  method       = "CBPS",
  pairs        = length(psmatch.cbps$index.treated),
  mean.diff    = mean(y_trt.cbps - y_con.cbps),
  OR           = exp(coef(gmodel9)["treatment.swang"]),
  OR.adjusted  = exp(coef(gmodel10)["treatment.swang"])))
print(effects, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)


print("===================================================")
```
For the RF model, the p-value values are all significant: for the t-test 0.0411, the McNemar test 0.04489, and the coefficient of the glm model has a significance value of 0.0398 and results in an odds ratio for treatment: 1.1632. After explicitly adjust for the highest SMD variable (Cirrhosis), the coefficient p-value actually decreased to 0.02805, and the odds ratio rises to 1.1757. For the NN model, the effect seems to be even stronger in all tests: the p-value for the t-test is 0.000416, for the McNemar test 0.000483, and the coefficient of the glm model has a significance value of 0.000324 and results in an odds ratio for treatment: 1.2929. After explicitly adjust for the highest SMD variable (wtkilo1), the coefficient p-value actually decreased to 0.000206, and the odds ratio again rises slightly to 1.3047. Lastly, for the CBPS model the treatment effects become even stronger: the p-value for the t-test is 4.184e-05, for the McNemar test 5.048e-05, and the coefficient of the glm model has a significance value of 4.36e-05  and results in an odds ratio for treatment: 1.3390. After explicitly adjust for the highest SMD variable (wtkilo1), the coefficient p-value is 8.35e-05, and the odds ratio again rises slightly to 1.3260. Comparing this to the original GLM propensity model, we see that the NN and CBPS obtain similar effect results, and also obtain similar mean difference results (close to the glm's approximate 0.06). The RF shows the mean difference lower at 0.03. However, all models still agree that there is significant evidence that treatment does affect outcome, and in fact the chance of dying increases with RHC treatment. Since the 4 propensity-based models balanced the data similarly well, we place roughly equal amounts of trust in their results. However, since we chose the original GLM-based propensity method as our preferred, conditional on our selected covariates capturing the relevant confounding, the glm-propensity-matched result is our best estimate, because it achieved the (marginally) best-balanced comparison among the methods we tested. Notably, the forest did not confirm our hypothesis that a threshold-based model would balance better, but it and all the other models do earn their place as a robustness check: they all still find higher mortality among treated patients, so the RHC result does not depend on the form of the logistic model Mahalanobis matching is the clear loser, with the most group imbalance and the estimate that shifted most under adjustment.


# Next, since the 4 propensity models balance similarly well, we want to try and dive a little bit deeper into why this is the case. Do they balance similarly well because they converge on the same distribution of propensity scores? Or do they each get different propensity scores but do the different scores happen to balance simiarly well. As stated at the start, we have no real interest in the propensity scores themselves, only their usage as a balancing tool, so probing this can help us understand the balancing mechanism better. 
```{r}
pscores.df <- data.frame(
  glm  = pscore,
  rf   = pscore.rf,
  nn   = pscore.nn,
  cbps = pscore.cbps
)
cor.matrix.pearson <- cor(pscores.df) #Perform Pearson (linear) correlation
cor.matrix.spearman <- cor(pscores.df, method = "spearman") #Perform Spearman (rank) correlation to check for relative ordering and not just numeric scale.

print(cor.matrix.pearson)
print(cor.matrix.spearman)

corrplot(cor.matrix.pearson, method = "color", type = "upper", addCoef.col = "black",
         title = "Pearson correlation between propensity scores across methods", mar = c(0,0,1,0))

corrplot(cor.matrix.spearman, method = "color", type = "upper", addCoef.col = "black",
         title = "Spearman correlation between propensity scores across methods", mar = c(0,0,1,0))

```
These correlation results reveal a clear pattern: the glm, NN, and CBPS propensity scores are all very highly correlated with each other (Pearson/Spearman both approximately 0.98–0.99), while RF stands notably apart, correlating with the other three at only 0.83–0.84. Note that both Pearson and Spearman agree with each other everywhere, so this isn't a scale-vs-ranking artifact, rather the RF genuinely ranks patients differently compared to the other models, not just on a different numeric scale. Importantly, this is consistent with our earlier reasoning about the models their functional forms: glm, NN, and CBPS all model treatment as some smooth, additive function of the covariates, while RF's completely different threshold-based, interaction-capturing splits produce a very different picture of who's likely treated. This divergence here is in correspondance with RF's comparatively worse SMD performance throughout our analysis; the model that thinks differently about the data is also the one that balances covariates least well, suggesting its threshold-based reasoning, whatever its clinical plausibility, isn't capturing the confounding structure as effectively as the smoother models are.



## Variable importance

To further probe this interesting difference in propensity value prediction strategies, we want to find out why and how each approach determines who gets treated. To do this, we will compare the variable importance of the GLM (our preferred model) and RF propensity prediction models.

For the glm we cannot simply compare the raw coefficients, because a coefficient is per unit of its variable (one year of age versus one point of APACHE score versus a 0/1 indicator), so instead we use the absolute z-value (coefficient divided by its standard error), which is scale-free and is exactly what the p-value in summary(psmodel) is based on. For the forest we use both the mean decrease in Gini impurity, i.e. how much splitting on a variable improved the purity of the treated/untreated mix, summed over every split in every tree, and the permutation importance which randomly permutes the values of a variables (removing any statisticaly relationship with the outcome) and then computes the decrease in accuracy. We do this because one caveat has to be kept in mind is that Gini importance is biased towards continuous variables, because a variable like meanbp1 or age offers a tree hundreds of candidate cutoffs whereas a 0/1 indicator like dnr1 offers exactly one, so the continuous variable has more possibilities to create an optimal split (and therefore be important), so the forest will naturally rank the continuous physiological measurements above the binary history and category variables. Lastly, since the two measures are on completely different scales, so we compare ranks rather than values.

```{r}
print("===================================================")
set.seed(42)
glm.abs.z <- abs(summary(psmodel)$coefficients[-1, "z value"])  # [-1] drops the intercept
imp.all   <- importance(rf.model)
rf.gini   <- imp.all[, "MeanDecreaseGini"]
rf.perm   <- imp.all[, "MeanDecreaseAccuracy"]

importance.comparison <- data.frame(
  glm.abs.z = round(glm.abs.z[xvars], 2),
  rf.gini   = round(rf.gini[xvars], 1),
  rf.perm   = round(rf.perm[xvars], 2)
)

importance.comparison$glm.rank      <- rank(-importance.comparison$glm.abs.z)  # rank 1 = most important
importance.comparison$rf.gini.rank  <- rank(-importance.comparison$rf.gini)
importance.comparison$rf.perm.rank  <- rank(-importance.comparison$rf.perm)

print(importance.comparison[order(importance.comparison$rf.gini.rank), ])

sprintf("Spearman correlation, glm vs RF Gini: %.2f",
        cor(importance.comparison$glm.abs.z, importance.comparison$rf.gini, method = "spearman"))
sprintf("Spearman correlation, glm vs RF permutation: %.2f",
        cor(importance.comparison$glm.abs.z, importance.comparison$rf.perm, method = "spearman"))
sprintf("Spearman correlation, RF Gini vs RF permutation: %.2f",
        cor(importance.comparison$rf.gini, importance.comparison$rf.perm, method = "spearman"))

varImpPlot(rf.model, n.var = 15, type = 1,
           main = "Random forest permutation importance (top 15)", cex = 0.6)
varImpPlot(rf.model, n.var = 15, type = 2,
           main = "Random forest Gini importance (top 15)", cex = 0.6)

print("===================================================")
```
The rank correlation tells us to what degree the two models look at the same variables: a value near 1 would mean they weigh the covariates in the same order as predictor, a value near 0 that their is no monotonic relationship between the ordering of the importance of the variables: knowing how important a variable is to glm gives you no information about how important it is to RF (and vice versa). A variable that the forest ranks high but the glm ranks low, and that is not simply continuous, is therefore the best candidate for a threshold or interaction effect that the additive glm cannot express. Since the balance after matching was nonetheless better for the GLM, whatever extra structure the forest picked up did not translate into a better propensity score, which is the same conclusion as before seen from the other side. 
In the results we can actually see a very interesting pattern. There are a few stand out disagreements (e.g. rea1 (creatinine): glm rank 30 (barely significant, z=1.11) vs. RF rank 3 (one of its top variables)) and a lot of moderate disagreements (e.g age: glm rank 38 (z=0.44, essentially not significant) vs. RF rank 6), resulting in a Spearman ranking correlation of only 0.14 for Gini and 0.33 for correlation. It initially sounds quite surprising that there is practically no correlation between the variable importance ranks, even though the propensity scores correlate at the much more significant 0.83. However, when looking closer we can see that the models agree on a small set of dominant predictors. For example, meanbp1 and aps1 both being in the top 1-3, having large z of approx. 8). These few dominant predictor dominate the predictions, which is enough to drive fairly high score correlation. Why certain variables are important for the RF model but not for the GLM (e.g. crea1 and age), can be because those variables do not correlate linearly with treatment, but once included in non-linar interactions or splits/thresholds, they can indeed become important. Lastly, it is notable that their is only a Spearman correlation of 0.61 between the RF Gini ranking and RF permutation ranking, indicating that the Gini importance was partly inflating the apparent RF/glm disagreement, likely due to its known bias toward continuous variables with many split points (as explained earlier). Once you switch to the less-biased permutation measure, RF and glm's importance rankings converge somewhat, though still far from strong agreement (0.33 is still weak).

#Partial dependence plot
To investigate why RF and glm disagreed sharply on dominant predictors for RF like crea1 and age (high RF importance, near-zero glm significance), we plotted partial dependence curves for both variables to try and probe/interpret the RF's model structure. This holds all other covariates at their observed values while sweeping the variable in questions across a range of values, and averaging each model's predicted propensity score. Both variables show visible nonlinear and threshold/step behavior in the RF, not the smooth trend a linear glm term would produce — confirming RF is genuinely capturing nonlinear structure the glm cannot express.
This is a nice nuance on our earlier finding that RF balanced worse than GLM despite this hypothesis. RF's threshold behavior is real, it just didn't help matching. This is likely because it also produced a rougher, more separated score distribution (consistent with RF's higher extreme-score counts and less correlated scores we saw before). So the intial "RF should balance better because it thinks like a clinician" hypothesis was right about the mechanism, but wrong about the practical payoff, which is a more interesting result, since it separates whether a model captures the expected structure from whether that structure helps the specific task of matching.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

partialPlot(rf.model, pred.data = rf.data, x.var = "crea1",
            main = "Partial dependence: crea1", xlab = "Creatinine (crea1)", ylab = "logit(P(treated))")

partialPlot(rf.model, pred.data = rf.data, x.var = "age",
            main = "Partial dependence: age", xlab = "Age", ylab = "logit(P(treated))")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


## Caliper width

Throughout the assignment we matched with a caliper of 0.2 standard deviations of the logit of the propensity score, which is the width recommended by Austin (2011), but we never checked whether that choice mattered, it was simply given to us by the instructors. The caliper is the knob that sets the bias-variance tradeoff of matching directly: a narrow caliper only accepts close matches, so the matched groups are well balanced (low bias), but more treated patients are left without a match, so the outcome effect estimate is based on fewer pairs (high variance) and, more subtly, on a different group of patients than the full treated population, as explained before. On the other hand, a wide caliper keeps nearly all treated patients but accepts poorer matches, so the imbalance creeps back in. Below we repeat the matching for a range of calipers, for all four propensity score models, and record the number of pairs, the balance and the resulting effect estimate given as the odds ratio from the GLM coefficient. Later, we perform a similar analysis for the greedy matching approach, but we do this seperately since it lives on an entirely different caliper scale as it is in 40D rather than 1D. 

```{r}
calipers <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 2)
logits.rf   <- logit(pmin(pmax(pscore.rf, 0.005), 0.995))
logits.nn   <- logit(pmin(pmax(pscore.nn, 0.005), 0.995))
logits.cbps <- logit(pmin(pmax(pscore.cbps, 0.005), 0.995))

caliper.comparison <- data.frame()

for (cal in calipers) {
  for (model in c("glm", "rf", "nn", "cbps")) {
    X.model <- switch(model,
                       glm  = logits,
                       rf   = logits.rf,
                       nn   = logits.nn,
                       cbps = logits.cbps)
    set.seed(42)
    mt <- Match(Tr = rhc.selected$treatment.swang, M = 1, X = X.model,
                replace = FALSE, Weight = 2, caliper = cal)
    md  <- rhc.selected[unlist(mt[c("index.treated", "index.control")]), ]
    smd <- ExtractSmd(CreateTableOne(vars = xvars, strata = "treatment.swang", data = md, test = FALSE))
    y.t <- md$outcome.died[md$treatment.swang == 1]
    y.c <- md$outcome.died[md$treatment.swang == 0]
    
    gmodel.cal <- glm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = binomial, data = md)
    coef.summary <- summary(gmodel.cal)$coefficients

    caliper.comparison <- rbind(caliper.comparison, data.frame(
      model          = model,
      caliper        = cal,
      matched.pairs  = length(mt$index.treated),
      max.smd        = round(max(smd), 3),
      n.smd.over.0.1 = sum(smd > 0.1),
      mean.diff      = round(mean(y.t - y.c), 3),
      OR             = round(exp(coef.summary["treatment.swang", "Estimate"]), 3),
      p.value        = signif(coef.summary["treatment.swang", "Pr(>|z|)"], 3)))
  }
}
print(caliper.comparison, row.names = FALSE)

ggplot(caliper.comparison, aes(x = caliper, y = matched.pairs, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "caliper (SD of logit PS, log scale)", y = "matched pairs", title = "Matched pairs kept vs caliper width") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(caliper.comparison, aes(x = caliper, y = max.smd, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() + scale_x_log10() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "caliper (SD of logit PS, log scale)", y = "max SMD", title = "Worst-variable SMD vs caliper width") +
  theme_minimal()
```
The two plots are the bias-variance tradeoff drawn out: the number of pairs rises with the caliper while the maximum SMD rises with it too, and the question is where the curves cross the point of diminishing returns. The sensible choice is the widest caliper that still keeps every variable under the dashed 0.1 line, since beyond that we are getting pairs with significant imbalance, and before that we are throwing away pairs without gaining much balance as the max-SMD plot is essentially flat for the first half. Notably, we see that the random forest model has a worse max SMD score and drops pairs faster throughout, highlighting its worse balancing performance as we demonstrated earlier. For the other three models, the optimal caliper seems to be around 0.75, which actually would have increased the number of matched pairs by around 200 for those models, significantly increasing the sample size to allow for smaller confidence intervals, less noisy estimates and more power to detect a real effect. Notably, in the results table we see that at this larger sample size the p-values are all still significant (5.65e-04 vs. 2.81e-02 vs. 1.16e-03 vs. 2.45e-05) and the odds ratios still indicate that the chance of dying increases with treatment (OR 1.266 vs. 1.166 vs. 1.247 vs. 1.334) for the GLM vs. RF vs. NN vs. CBPS. respectively.


Regarding the greedy matching with the Mahalanobis distance; we already observed that it obtains 0 matches using a caliper due to the matching happening in 40D. Moreover, it is interpreted as the variation in each covariate in standardized units of that covariate, rather than the variation in the logit of a predicted scalar - the caliper means very different things in each of the cases. As a result, the caliper range needsa completely different variation scale and shouldn't be compared directly with the other calipers, which is why we gave it it's own brief analysis here. 
```{r}
calipers.maha <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20)  # far larger, since caliper applies per-covariate across 40 dimensions
maha.comparison <- data.frame()

for (cal in calipers.maha) {
  set.seed(42)
  mt <- Match(Tr = rhc.selected$treatment.swang, M = 1, X = as.matrix(rhc.selected[xvars]),
              replace = FALSE, Weight = 2, caliper = cal)
  
  if (!is.list(mt) || is.null(mt$index.treated)) {
    maha.comparison <- rbind(maha.comparison, data.frame(
      caliper = cal, matched.pairs = 0, max.smd = NA, n.smd.over.0.1 = NA, mean.diff = NA, OR = NA))
    next
  }
  
  md  <- rhc.selected[unlist(mt[c("index.treated", "index.control")]), ]
  smd <- ExtractSmd(CreateTableOne(vars = xvars, strata = "treatment.swang", data = md, test = FALSE))
  y.t <- md$outcome.died[md$treatment.swang == 1]
  y.c <- md$outcome.died[md$treatment.swang == 0]
  
  gmodel.cal <- glm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = binomial, data = md)
  coef.summary <- summary(gmodel.cal)$coefficients

  maha.comparison <- rbind(maha.comparison, data.frame(
    caliper        = cal,
    matched.pairs  = length(mt$index.treated),
    max.smd        = round(max(smd), 3),
    n.smd.over.0.1 = sum(smd > 0.1),
    mean.diff      = round(mean(y.t - y.c), 3),
    OR             = round(exp(coef.summary["treatment.swang", "Estimate"]), 3),
    p.value        = signif(coef.summary["treatment.swang", "Pr(>|z|)"], 3)))
}
print(maha.comparison, row.names = FALSE)
```
In the results table above, we can see a few interesting results. First, we see that as the caliper is increased significantly, in range of 5+, we do get a significant amount of matches, meaning that in that case most treated patients do find at least 1 (unmatched) control where each of the 40 variables differ by no more than 5 standardized units. Notably, the p-values here also get small (in the range of e-10), and the odds ratio indicates, again, a positive result (death chances increase with treatment), though the OR is a lot larger than before: approximately 1.5 here whereas the other model were in the range of 1.1-1.3. However, we also observe that the number of variables with SMD above 0.1 is still 16 (which is more than at smaller calipers since the matches allowed are worse, per the bias-variance tradeoff discussed above), and the max smd stays around 0.5, which raises significant concerns regarding confounding. Considering this, even at higher calipers, getting larger amounts of matches, we still prefer the other models as the balancing of the covariates between the two groups is significantly better for those methods, allowing us to place significantly more trust in our obtained results.

# Inverse probability weighting (IPW)
Throughout this entire report, we simply assumed the matching strategy given to us at the start. However, maybe this is not the optimal strategy to use and do other strategies achieve better or similar balancing quality, while preserving more matched pairs. As such, as a last experiment, we try out an alternative to matching: inverse probability weighting. Here, all treated observations get a weight of 1, while the untreated observations get weighted by their odds of being treated (odds of the propensity score). Thus, untreated patients who look very likely to be treated are upweighted, since they are likely rare among the untreated, while untreated patients which don't look like treated pateints get downweighted, since they are common among this group. As a result, the weighted distribution of covariates of the untreated group is reshaped to look very similar to that of the treated group, (hopefully) achieving balancing of each covariates, the same result that matching tries to achieve. Then, all patients are used in a weighted manner in the downstream outcome effect analysis. This allows us to isolate and compare each model's own balancing quality, without relying on the matching step to drop bad quality matches. 
```{r}
compute_att_weights <- function(ps, treatment) {
  ifelse(treatment == 1, 1, ps / (1 - ps))
}

pscores.list <- list(
  glm  = pscore,
  rf   = pscore.rf,
  nn   = pscore.nn,
  cbps = pscore.cbps
)

ipw.comparison <- data.frame()

for (name in names(pscores.list)) {
  ps.c <- pmin(pmax(pscores.list[[name]], 0.005), 0.995)
  w <- compute_att_weights(ps.c, rhc.selected$treatment.swang)
  
  design.w <- svydesign(ids = ~1, data = rhc.selected[, c(xvars, "treatment.swang", "outcome.died")], weights = ~w)
  
  # Balance check as before
  tab.weighted <- svyCreateTableOne(vars = xvars, strata = "treatment.swang", data = design.w, test = FALSE)
  smd.weighted <- ExtractSmd(tab.weighted)
  
  # Test treatment effect on outcome, using the same weights design
  m <- svyglm(outcome.died ~ treatment.swang, family = quasibinomial, design = design.w)
  cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
  
  ipw.comparison <- rbind(ipw.comparison, data.frame(
    model           = name,
    max.smd         = round(max(smd.weighted), 3),
    n.smd.under.0.1 = sum(smd.weighted < 0.1),
    n.smd.0.1.0.2   = sum(smd.weighted >= 0.1 & smd.weighted < 0.2),
    n.smd.over.0.2  = sum(smd.weighted > 0.2),
    max.weight      = round(max(w), 1),
    OR              = round(exp(cf["treatment.swang", "Estimate"]), 3),
    p.value         = signif(cf["treatment.swang", "Pr(>|t|)"], 3)))
}
print(ipw.comparison, row.names = FALSE)
```
In these results we observe similar trends as before. Notably, the balancing of RF is, again, the worst with a max smd = 0.11 and 2 variables over 0.1. The other methods perform similar, however the glm propensity prediction model does seem to fall behind a bit with a max smd = 0.1 and 1 variables over 0.1, whereas with regular matching its max smd was only 0.035 (and thus 0 variables over 0.1). This might suggest that that model was helped relatively a lot by the matching step disposing of bad untreated patients. Moreover, here the p-values are also all significant and comparable to the ones obtained with matching, the same for the odds ratios. 
However, as a general approach matching does seem to be preferable over IPW, since it does lead to better matching and does not reduce the power of the outcome analysis significantly, as we just compared. 


# Final Conclusions
In conclusion, after deep and thoughtful analysis of different propensity prediction models used for matching, including probing of various properties of them, and looking at an alternatives to the standard matching architecture we were given initially, we arrive at one most favourable approach. The intial GLM (logistic regression) propensity prediction model is the preferred model of choice as it: 1. produced the best overall balancing of each covariate across the treated and non-treated groups, and 2. it is the more simplistic and consequently interpretable model, as we can look at its standardized coefficients to directly get an accurate idea of the role each variable plays in its predictions, as opposed to, for example, the neural network whose weights are much more a blackbox. Moreover, we observed that matching with a slightly better caliper (approximately 0.75 standardized units) would allow for more matches, and consequently more power and less noisy estimates in the downstream outcome analysis, while hardly reducing the balancing is the best balancing approach, and preferred over direct inverse probability weighting. This preferred approach led to an odds ratio of 1.266 with a p-value of 5.65e-04, suggesting that their is enough evidence to conclude that RHC treatment increase the odds of dying, assuming the ignorability assumption holds.



#References
Austin, P. C. (2011). Optimal caliper widths for propensity-score matching when estimating differences in means and differences in proportions in observational studies. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 10(2), 150-161.

Imai, K., & Ratkovic, M. (2014). Covariate balancing propensity score. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 76(1), 243-263.
